questions.q: What does this lesson identify as the core problem with a traditional VPN, even when the user authenticates correctly?
options: VPNs cannot encrypt traffic over the public internet
VPNs place the device onto the broader network, so whatever the network allows becomes reachable, not just the one app the user needed
VPNs are too expensive for most organizations to license
VPNs require a hardware token for every connection attempt
questions.explain: A VPN's job effectively ends at granting network reachability — once connected, the user can reach whatever the network itself permits, which is almost always broader than the one application they actually needed.

questions.q: What is the defining property of a software-defined perimeter (SDP), as described in this lesson?
options: The application stays cloaked and unreachable until a request has already been authenticated and authorized
It requires every user to be issued a static public IP address
It replaces identity verification with network-location checks
It only works for applications hosted on a single named cloud provider
questions.explain: SDP's defining idea is "default deny, cloaked until authorized" — an application behind an SDP doesn't even respond to an unauthorized connection attempt, so it appears not to exist to anyone unauthorized.

questions.q: In a typical ZTNA deployment, what does the connector running inside the private network do?
options: It opens an inbound firewall port so the broker can reach it directly
It replaces the application's own authentication system entirely
It broadcasts the application's existence to the public internet for discovery
It makes an outbound-only connection to the broker, so no inbound firewall rule has to be opened
questions.explain: The connector initiates an outbound-only connection to the cloud broker, which is why no inbound port ever needs to be opened on the private network's firewall.

questions.q: Which of the following are given in this lesson as real products in the ZTNA category?
options: CyberArk, Azure PIM, and a generic password vault
Azure Firewall, AWS Network Firewall, and a Transit Gateway
Zscaler Private Access, Cloudflare Access, and Microsoft Entra Private Access
Terraform, Bicep, and a generic ARM template
questions.explain: The lesson names Zscaler Private Access, Cloudflare Access, and Microsoft Entra Private Access as real examples of the broker-and-connector ZTNA pattern.

questions.q: How does this lesson connect ZTNA back to the micro-segmentation idea from Lesson 9?
options: It argues ZTNA has nothing in common with micro-segmentation
It claims micro-segmentation only applies to on-premises networks, never to remote access
Both shrink the unit that policy grants reachability to — from a whole network segment down to one workload or one application — instead of granting broad access by default
It claims ZTNA replaces the need for workload identity entirely
questions.explain: Lesson 9 shrank network policy to a single workload; this lesson shows ZTNA doing the same shrinking for remote user access, scoping a session down to exactly one application instead of a whole network segment.
